sentence: With nearly 60% of its population under the age of 25¹, Africa represents the world's largest concentration of young people.

They are part of a major demographic and territorial transformation: according to the Economic Report on Africa 2017 by the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA/UNECA), the share of the African population living in urban areas has increased from 31% in 1990 to a projected 49% in 2035.

Cross-estimated data from studies conducted by the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA), Injini, and EdTech Hub places the current size of the African market between USD 600 million and USD 1 billion, a very modest figure compared to the USD 300 billion global EdTech market.

Despite this low capitalization, the development prospects are particularly encouraging: Projected annual growth of between 15% and 20% by 2035, supported by increasing demand for digital learning services.

The rise of flexible learning methods, including online training, micro-credentials, and short professional programs; mobile penetration exceeding 90% in several African countries, paving the way for "mobile-first" models³; more than 600 active tech hubs across the continent, forming a growing network for incubation and innovation⁴ The COVID-19 pandemic has also acted as an unprecedented accelerator.
Less than 2% of technology venture capital invested in Africa is directed towards EdTech¹, placing this sector far behind fintech, e- commerce, or e-health.

Three countries stand out clearly and together account for almost 60% of all responses collected.

Benin comes out on top with 27.8% of respondents, confirming the emergence of a particularly active EdTech ecosystem, supported by public policies favorable to educational innovation, the presence of structuring support structures and a strong mobilization of entrepreneurs in the sector.
Ivory Coast represents 16.7% of the responses, reflecting the gradual rise of EdTech solutions in a context marked by increasing investments in digital education and vocational training.

Senegal, with 13.9% of respondents, stands out as a strategic hub, benefiting from a structured institutional framework around the Digital Senegal Strategy, SIMEN and regional initiatives such as the timbuktoo program and the prospect of the Dakar EdTech Hub.

Profile and dynamics of the EdTech ecosystem analyzed The EdTech ecosystem studied is primarily composed of startups (53%) and SMEs (31%), reflecting a sector that is still young, innovative, but in a phase of structuring.
The presence of NGOs (11%) also underscores a strong focus on social impact and educational inclusion.
The representation of women is generally heterogeneous but encouraging, with many organizations having between 30% and 50% women, and a few cases of high feminization (>60%).
In terms of offerings, the ecosystem is heavily geared towards educational content (36%) and TVET/skills/employability (22%), segments that are quicker to deploy and less capital-intensive.
The ecosystem is dominated by continuing education/workforce/skills (66.7%), followed by K-12 (55.6%) and higher education (41.7%).
TVET is well represented (36.1%), while early childhood education remains a minority (22.2%).
Priorities are focused on digital learning (LMS/LXP – 63.9%) and content & curriculum (58.3%).
These are followed by assessment/certification and well-being & inclusion (36.1% each).
Management systems (SIS/ERP – 22.2%) and education financing (11.1%) are underrepresented.
The dominant cluster is Upskilling / Bootcamps / Short courses (58.3%).
For K-12s, Content & Curriculum (30.6%) and Management/Data (22.2%) stand out.
In post-secondary education, student support (27.8%) is more popular than management systems (13.9%).
The solutions primarily focus on AI (recommendations, chatbots) and interactive/immersive content (36.1% each), reflecting a strong emphasis on the learning experience and personalization.
Analytics and dashboards occupy an intermediate position (19.4%), while system interoperability (APIs, SIS, EMIS) and payment/EdFin remain marginally addressed.
Learners and parents are the primary target audience (47.1%), followed by educational institutions (35.3%).
Businesses (11.8%) and governments/ministries remain secondary.
Coverage is relatively balanced between primary, secondary, and TVET/training centers (approximately 19% each).
Colleges are less covered (11.1%), while universities/higher education institutions and businesses/government agencies each represent 13.9%.
